text.p: Tobacco to insurance company B.A.T Industries Plc dismissed on Friday a Mississippi court ruling against the tobacco industry as purely procedural.

But investors took fright in the wake of a string of lawsuits by smokers against the American tobacco industry, sending the shares of both Imperial Tobacco Group Plc and B.A.T in London sharply lower.

"It is a purely procedural decision; all the court has done is to decide not to decide the issues now, it is not a decision on the merits of the case at all," said B.A.T company spokesman Michael Prideaux.
"We are confident that ultimately we will win the case," he added.
Brown & Williamson, a subsidiary of B.A.T, has about 17 percent of the U.S. cigarette market and is one of the defendants in the case along with Philip Morris Cos Inc and RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co.
The Mississippi Supreme Court threw out challenges by Governor Kirk Fordice and the tobacco industry that would have kept the $940 million historic case from proceeding to trial on June 2.
It is the first of 22 such suits filed by state attorneys general across the U.S. to recoup Medicaid healthcare costs.
But the Mississippi decision does not mean all these other Medicaid cases will now be heard, said Prideaux.

The decision sent the shares of tobacco companies sharply lower, with Philip Morris Cos off $10.75 to $126 on Thursday. In London B.A.T shares dropped 31 pence at the opening to 523-1/2p before clawing back half the decline. Shares in Imperial Tobacco, demerged from Hanson Plc in October 1996, were off 5p at 433p.
"We take a watching interest but it has no impact on us operationally or legally because we don't have any American exposure," said Imperial's legal manager Alan Porter.
Nyren Scott-Malden, analyst at BZW, said he thought the fall in tobacco shares had been overdone on both sides of the Atlantic, exaggerated by nervousness about the Dow's steep slide on Thursday.
"It has been a gross over-reaction on the part of both the U.S. market and the UK market to news on a bad day," he said.
Another analyst said the ruling had provided a reason to take profits after a strong run by tobacco shares.

"Clearly what last night's news has done is get back into people's thinking that litigation has to be paid attention to," he said. "All these shares have had a great run and this provided a temptation to take profits."
The Carter case was a suit against a B.A.T unit by a smoker who sued for damages resulting from smoking. A Florida jury awarded Grady Carter and his wife Millie $750,000 in damages last August.
Amanda Sandford, spokeswoman for ASH, the campaign for freedom from tobacco, hailed the decision as offering considerable hope to smokers.

"The tobacco company's attempts to manipulate the legal process has clearly failed and we look forward to the full trial in June, then we will see just how disreputable the industry really is," she said.
